newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea summons Kim's aide, lawmakers over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea summons Kim's aide, lawmakers over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors summoned three politicians, including a close associate of President Kim Young-sam, for questioning on Monday over huge loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co, a prosecution official said.

Widening their probe into a loan scandal that has shocked South Korea and put the heat on Kim in a presidential election year, prosecutors said they wanted to determine if politicians pressured bankers into extending loans to Hanbo Steel.

In a bid to limit fallout from the scandal, the government on Monday promised steps to limit its impact on the economy. It set aside 1.4 trillion won ($1.6 billion) to aid Hanbo suppliers and other small firms suffering from a credit crunch, the Finance and Economy Ministry said in a statement.
"Prosecutors will focus their investigation on whether there were political pressures on bankers or kickbacks involved," a prosecution official told Reuters.

Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog told reporters that Hong In-gil, a lawmaker of the ruling New Korea Party and a senior official at the presidential Blue House until last year, was quizzed on whether he had received kickbacks from Hanbo.
Also summoned by prosecutors were Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, and Chung Jae-chull from the ruling party.
Hong and Chung reported to prosecutors on Monday but Kwon told them that he would appear at their office on Tuesday.

The three were the first politicians to be probed over loans totalling five trillion won ($5.8 billion) provided to Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, before it was declared insolvent on January 23.
President Kim last month ordered a probe into loans. He has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.
Prosecutors have already arrested Chung Tae-soo, founder of the Hanbo Group and its steelmaking flagship, and two leading bankers over the loan scandal.
Hong, who has been President Kim's aide for more than two decades, has denied taking money from Hanbo.

Kwon, a leading member of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, said he had nothing to do with Hanbo loans. But he has said he took between 150 million and 160 million won from Hanbo, partly to fund an election campaign.
The other lawmaker has not publicly commented.
Prosecutors also summoned Chung Bo-keun, the Hanbo founder's son and now current group chairman, for questioning, Choi said.

Opposition parties have accused the government of peddling influence for the loans that allowed Hanbo Group to emerge as South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding its steelmaking flagship and by acquiring or setting up 18 firms over the past three years.
The National Congress on Monday urged the president to make a public apology for the scandal, calling it "Hanbogate".
"The ultimate responsibility for Hanbogate lies on President Kim Young-sam," it said in a statement.
State radio said about half a dozen other politicians, including some tipped as contenders in December's presidential polls, were due to be summoned by prosecutors.
Prosecutors declined to confirm the radio report.
Political analysts said the Hanbo scandal could have a major impact on the presidential elections.

"Unless the probe into Hanbo loans produces a convincing outcome, the president's morality would be questioned and the prospects for the ruling camp would be dismal," Cho Chang-hyun, political science professor at Hanyang University, said.
President Kim is barred from seeking re-election, but analysts expect him to seek to install a protege.

The president gave top priority to rooting out corruption after he took office in 1993, but his anti-graft drive has been hurt in the past year following the arrest of several of his top officials, including a defence minister, on bribery charges. ($1= 867 won)
